It's the fundamental structure through which information is transmitted from one neuron to another. ↵ ↵ Here is a detailed breakdown of what happens at a synapse, step-by-step: ↵ ↵ --- ↵ ↵ The Process of Synaptic Transmission ↵ ↵ Synaptic transmission is a complex, rapid process that converts an electrical signal (the action potential) in the presynaptic neuron into a chemical signal that the postsynaptic neuron can understand. ↵ ↵ Phase 1: Arrival of the Signal (The Electrical Event) ↵ ↵ 1. Action Potential Arrival: An electrical impulse (an action potential) travels down the axon of the presynaptic neuron (the sending neuron). ↵ 2. Voltage Change: When the action potential reaches the end of the axon, it causes a rapid change in the electrical potential across the presynaptic terminal (the axon terminal). ↵ ↵ Phase 2: Neurotransmitter Release (The Chemical Event) ↵ ↵ 3. Calcium Influx: The change in voltage opens specialized voltage-gated calcium channels located on the presynaptic terminal membrane. ↵ 4. Calcium Entry: Because the concentration of calcium ions (\text{Ca}^{2+}) is much higher outside the cell, \text{Ca}^{2+} rushes *into* the presynaptic terminal. ↵ 5. Vesicle Fusion: The influx of \text{Ca}^{2+} acts as a trigger. It causes synaptic vesicles (tiny sacs filled with neurotransmitters) to move toward and fuse with the presynaptic membrane. ↵ 6.
